| [LIT-031](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-031.md) v2 | Moving away from lexicalism in psycho- and neuro-linguistics | Krauska & Lau (2023), DOI-10.3389/flang.2023.1125127. The authors argue that lemma-based production models encode two lexicalist assumptions: a morphology/syntax split, and a stored meaning–syntax–form "triad". Updating the representations (treelets) is not enough, because the algorithms — separate lexical retrieval and structure building, word-sized increments — also have to change. They sketch an 8-stage non-lexicalist model and derive qualitative aphasia predictions from it. | [LIT-046](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-046.md) v3 | The Computational Foundations of Collective Intelligence | Pilgrim et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2509.07999](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07999). A conceptual framework, with no model, data or derivation. It sets out individual and collective computational resources in four dimensions: sensing ΣI_i, states S_c × ∏S_i, processes F_c + ΣF_i, and actions ∏A_i (Table 1). It then maps the collective's surplus onto familiar mechanisms (aggregation with noise σ_i²/n, distributional beliefs P(H), memory persistence T_c, division of labour). From it the authors derive 14 indicator properties: RPT-1–2, GWT-1–4, HOT-1–4, AST-1, PP-1 and AE-1–2. The claim for them is only that more of them raises the probability of consciousness. They assess a handful of systems against subsets of the list and conclude that no current system "appears to be a strong candidate". Transformer LLMs have "only a relatively weak case" for any GWT indicator, because a single forward pass has no recurrence or global broadcast. | [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) v3 | The Extended Mind | Clark & Chalmers (1998), DOI-10.1093/analys/58.1.7. The paper argues from a functionalist parity claim that a process or standing state which would count as cognitive if it happened in the head counts as cognitive when an external resource carries it, provided the resource is actively coupled to the organism here and now. The four "criteria" for a coupled resource (constancy, direct availability, automatic endorsement, and the admittedly "arguable" past conscious endorsement) are offered as the features that make the paradigm case clear. | [LIT-105](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-105.md) v3 | On the Evolution, Science, and Metaphysics of Consciousness | Veit (2025), DOI-10.1177/10597123251413204. Veit's reply to five commentaries on *A Philosophy for the Science of Animal Consciousness* (2023). Its main new content is the metaphysics the book left to one paragraph. He says hedonic "feel" is *identical* with a valence system: "a common currency of sharing evaluative information across multiple control systems". The currency metaphor, he says, is "not Cartesian but cybernetic" (p. 10). He keeps the word "qualia", arguing that Cartesians have no "definitional rights" (p. 9), and he insists the pathological complexity thesis (PCT) is compatible with any metaphysics, dualism and panpsychism included (p. 9). Against his other critics, he defends a bottom-up evolutionary method that uses human data (de Weerd); a naturalism that is neither autopoietic nor biopsychist (Sachs); evaluation-first over prediction-first, consciousness as an adaptation, and graded, partial unity (Suzuki); and the link to welfare science (Chincarini). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-187](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-187.md)); worth reading as the only extended statement of the metaphysics behind the pathological complexity thesis, and as the direct answer to Frankish ([LIT-103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-103.md)). The reply to Frankish is the substantive part. The replies to de Weerd and Suzuki mostly restate the book's positions against objections quoted only in part, so read them alongside the commentaries. |

| [LIT-140](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-140.md) v2 | Large Language Models Are Stochastic Measuring Devices | Mallory (2025), DOI-10.1093/9780191998317.003.0003. The chapter argues by analogy that deep neural networks are "stochastic measuring devices". Training alters the parameters in response to data, so that the resulting configuration carries information about the data ("training is measurement"). The trained weights are a model, and generation is simulation. DNNs are stochastic because random initialisation and non-convex loss mean runs need not converge to the same weights, failing Baird's "regularity" condition. The problems of interpreting model states and generated text are therefore the familiar problems of instruments, models and simulations. The problem of interpretable AI is an instance of the coordination problem in the philosophy of measurement. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-090](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-090.md)); worth reading as the most developed instrument-centred alternative to agentive framings of LLMs, and for its tidy division into model-interpretation, text-interpretation and linking problems; it offers an analogy, not a refutation (its own words, § Interpretation and Communication), and should be read in the published OUP version where possible. |
| [LIT-147](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-147.md) v3 | Mental causation via neuroprosthetics? A critical analysis | Pernu (2018), DOI-10.1007/s11229-018-1713-z. The interventionist/difference-making case for nonreductive mental causation from BCIs (List & Menzies 2009; Menzies 2015; Woodward 2008a,b, 2017) misplaces multiple realisation. What the ensemble recordings show is that one cortical-level variable N (the ensemble's average firing) is realised by many single-neuron patterns N1, N2. Each intention M corresponds to one value of N. So the counterfactual contrast "∼M □→ ∼B true, ∼N □→ ∼B false" fails, and neuroprosthetics supports mental causation only by identifying M with N, not nonreductive physicalism. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-091](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-091.md)); Worth reading as a short, precise diagnosis of a specific equivocation in the interventionist BCI argument (multiple realisation at the wrong level). Its scope is limited to difference-making with a proportionality constraint (fn 1), and its identity conclusion rests on a simplified picture of neural decoding that it asserts rather than argues. |

The decisive HHH vs HHH+0 comparison is a conjecture that the authors say needs further empirical work. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-138](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-138.md)); Worth reading as the clearest statement of interpretationist realism about LLM instance agents. It turns "does it want?" into comparisons of rival desire hypotheses against named behavioural results, and it is candid that its central empirical discriminations are untested. |
| [LIT-207](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-207.md) v2 | Talkative AI and the fiction of artificial minds | Roberts (2026), DOI-10.1007/s11098-026-02560-8. If a substantial class of mental states (interoceptive, affective, perceptual, and bodily-agentive states such as effort, trying and ownership) depends on an animate body, then today's disembodied chatbots lack them, and their many self-ascriptions of such states are "systematically untrue". Roberts argues that users can nonetheless engage chatbots through make-believe, as a new kind of fictional character that is interactive, co-constructed, self-involving and blended with the real world. He argues that this fictionalist stance escapes the epistemic norms that bind realist belief. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-157](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-157.md)); worth reading as a short, clear statement of chatbot fictionalism. Its anti-realist premise is explicitly conditional and targets only body-dependent states, which leaves belief and reasoning open. |
| [LIT-212](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-212.md) v2 | Do Large Language Models Hallucinate Electric Fata Morganas? | Šekrst (2025), [ARXIV-2608.18816](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18816). A conceptual essay whose one substantive thesis is this. Following Dziri et al., hallucination includes any output "not rooted in the model's source data", including expressed emotions and opinions (§6). An LLM's apparent inner life is therefore always a candidate hallucination, so any real AI consciousness "might always remain epistemically inaccessible" (§8). The empirical support is two unquantified anecdotes: a Titanic question put to gpt-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 at unstated temperatures, and an extractive-QA BERT mislabelled "WikiBERT". Neither can bear the weight the paper puts on it. | Rejected — read in full 2026-09-26 (NOTE-176); not worth a reader's time. Its one idea, that self-reports of inner states are exactly what a system trained on human text would produce whether or not it has them, is a single paragraph's point. Its experiments are anecdotes with no reported settings, one of them on a mislabelled model. It asserts both that current LLMs lack understanding and that machine consciousness would be undetectable, and never reconciles the two. |
| [LIT-220](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-220.md) v2 | Real Patterns | Dennett (1991), DOI-10.2307/2027085. A pattern is real in some data "if there is a description of the data that is more efficient than the bit map, whether or not anyone can concoct it" (p. 34). This is Chaitin's incompressibility definition of randomness turned around (p. 32). Dennett uses the criterion, with the Game of Life's gliders and eaters as the stepping stone (pp. 37–42), to defend "mild realism" about beliefs. Folk psychology tracks a real, noisy pattern of enormous predictive leverage. Two rival interpretations can be "different, but equally real, patterns" with no deeper fact to settle between them (p. 49). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-190](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-190.md)); Worth reading as the source of the real-patterns criterion that rainforest realism generalises into a theory of existence, and as the paper whose exact definition the later literature modifies. It has a lossless-compression criterion, observer-relativity through "perspectives", and trade-offs between noise and simplicity. Its target is beliefs, not ontology in general. Dennett explicitly declines the label question ("I think that the view itself is clearer than either of the labels", p. 51). |
